title: Asteroid Flyby: 2026 WU1 Passed Earth at 12.5 Lunar Distances, Size Estimate Spans 98 to 220 Feet
excerpt: Asteroid flyby 2026 WU1 passed Earth at 12.5 lunar distances late Thursday, Nov. 26, ET, but NASA’s JPL lists no measured diameter for the near-Earth asteroid. Its 98 to 220 foot size estimate depends on assumed surface reflectivity, JPL’s dashboard shows 130 feet, and the pass carried no impact
content:
Asteroid 2026 WU1 passed Earth at about 11:32 p.m. ET Thursday, Nov. 26 (04:32 UTC Friday), at a distance of 4.82 million kilometers (3.0 million miles), or 12.5 times the average Earth-Moon distance, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), whose close-approach table lists the pass. JPL's small-body database lists no measured diameter, so any size for the object is an estimate from its brightness, and depending on how dark its surface is, that estimate runs from about 30 meters (98 feet) to 67 meters (220 feet).

The pass carried no impact risk. The open question is the size, and JPL's public Asteroid Watch dashboard shows one figure, 130 feet (40 meters). The dashboard gives no estimation method, but its number matches what a 14% surface reflectivity would produce, the value NASA's near-Earth object program uses for size estimates: 40 meters (132 feet).

Pan-STARRS 1, a 1.8-meter (5.9-foot) telescope on Haleakalā in Hawaii, is credited with the discovery in the Minor Planet Center's notice MPEC 2026-W76, dated Nov. 21, five days before the pass. JPL's entry lists no discovery details, and its orbit solution uses 15 observations dated Nov. 19 to Nov. 21, two days of data.

How Big Is Asteroid 2026 WU1? Absolute Magnitude 24.7 Depends on Albedo Assumption

Absolute magnitude, written H, is how bright an asteroid would look at 1 astronomical unit (about 93 million miles) from both the Sun and the observer, in ideal alignment. JPL lists 2026 WU1 at H 24.7, with an uncertainty of about 0.5.

Turning H into a diameter takes a second number, albedo, the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. A dark surface (albedo 0.05) gives 2026 WU1 a diameter of about 67 meters (220 feet), the 0.14 value NASA assumes gives 40 meters (132 feet), and a bright surface (0.25) gives 30 meters (98 feet), according to TechTimes calculations using the standard conversion and JPL's H value. Adding the uncertainty in H itself widens the full span to roughly 24 to 84 meters (79 to 275 feet).

The ambiguity is built into the physics: a dark object absorbs light that a bright one reflects, so two asteroids of different sizes can look equally bright from Earth. Real asteroid albedos range from about 0.05 to 0.30, which can leave a diameter off by a factor of 2 and a volume off by a factor of 8.

Webb Infrared Data Narrowed Asteroid 2024 YR4 From 40 to 90 Meters to 53 to 67 Meters

When asteroid 2024 YR4 was first found, early observations put its size at 40 to 90 meters (131 to 295 feet). Infrared observations by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope in March 2025 then narrowed it to 174 to 220 feet (53 to 67 meters). The current bracket for 2026 WU1 is about as wide as the one Webb narrowed.

NASA's NEO Surveyor space telescope is built for this gap. Its telescope observes two heat-sensing infrared wavelengths, which let it detect dark asteroids as well as bright ones. JPL says it will launch no earlier than September 2027, and its five-year baseline survey is meant to find at least two-thirds of near-Earth objects larger than 140 meters (460 feet).

The mission's money is still being settled. Federal agencies are operating under a continuing resolution that expires Dec. 11, and the House Appropriations Committee's fiscal 2027 bill provides $283.7 million for NEO Surveyor.

Three Institutions Turned One Pan-STARRS Detection Into JPL's Close-Approach Prediction

Pan-STARRS, two 1.8-meter (5.9-foot) telescopes on Haleakalā whose operating costs are mostly paid by NASA through its Near-Earth Object Observations program, finds asteroids by their motion against background stars across repeated images.

The Minor Planet Center, which works under the International Astronomical Union at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, collects those positions, publishes discovery circulars and calculates orbits. Its Nov. 21 notice for 2026 WU1 credited five observatory codes, including both Pan-STARRS telescopes. JPL's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies then computes high-precision orbits and the close approaches that appear in its public table.

Condition Code 7: Pass Geometry Is Tight, Long-Term Orbit Is Loose

JPL's orbit for 2026 WU1 rests on 15 observations over two days and carries a condition code of 7 on a 0-to-9 scale, where higher numbers mean a less certain orbit. The scale estimates how far an orbit's predicted position could drift after 10 years, and the Minor Planet Center cautions that it is not a predictor of future motion for near-Earth objects.

The pass itself is a different matter. JPL's 3-sigma distance range runs from 4.80 million kilometers (2.98 million miles) to 4.85 million kilometers (3.01 million miles), a span of about 49,000 kilometers (30,500 miles), and the 3-sigma timing uncertainty is about 2 minutes. Questions about its long-term path stay open until more observations arrive, since orbit accuracy improves with more observations.

JPL classifies 2026 WU1 as Apollo-class, meaning its orbit crosses Earth's path while its average distance from the Sun is larger than Earth's. It circles the Sun every 460 days (1.26 years), from 0.70 astronomical units (about 65 million miles) inside Earth's orbit out to 1.64 astronomical units (about 152 million miles), and its Earth minimum orbit intersection distance is 0.024 astronomical units, about 3.6 million kilometers (2.3 million miles).

The asteroid does not qualify as potentially hazardous. That label requires an orbit intersection distance of 0.05 astronomical units or less and an absolute magnitude of about 22 or brighter, roughly 140 meters (460 feet) or larger, and 2026 WU1 meets only the distance test.

Six Asteroids Passed Within 19.5 Lunar Distances in 63 Hours, With 2026 WU1 Last

JPL's close-approach table lists six asteroids inside 0.05 astronomical units (19.5 lunar distances) between Nov. 24 and Nov. 26, the first at 8:58 a.m. ET Tuesday and the last 2026 WU1.

JPL lists those times in Barycentric Dynamical Time, which runs about 69 seconds ahead of UTC, so TechTimes converted each to ET. JPL's documentation describes the speed column as relative to the approach body, here Earth.

The smallest of the group, 2026 WX1, is listed at 34 feet (10 meters) on JPL's dashboard, and the same albedo calculation from its H of 27.6 brackets it at 8 to 18 meters (27 to 60 feet).

The table shows only what surveys have found. One 2016 estimate counted about 840,000 objects near 40 meters (131 feet) in size, of which about 1.3% were known.

Chelyabinsk's 20-Meter Asteroid Injured 1,500 People, Far Below NASA's 140-Meter Search Target

NASA's congressionally set search goal covers near-Earth objects of 140 meters (460 feet) or larger, so 2026 WU1's estimated 30 to 67 meters (98 to 220 feet) falls below it. Size still matters below that line: the roughly 20-meter (66-foot) asteroid that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 injured an estimated 1,500 people with flying glass. Impacts by 60-meter (197-foot) objects are estimated at roughly once every 1,300 years.

NASA planetary defense officer Kelly Fast told the American Association for the Advancement of Science in February that about 25,000 asteroids larger than 140 meters orbit near Earth and NASA has located about 40% of them. UCLA astronomer Amy Mainzer, who leads NEO Surveyor, has said that smaller asteroids can still cause damage and that scientists do not know where most of them are.

For 2026 WU1, the verified facts are the pass itself: 3.0 million miles away, timed to within about 2 minutes, with no impact risk. The unverified fact is the size. JPL's records list no diameter, the 98-to-220-foot range rests on an assumed reflectivity, and JPL's dashboard condenses it to 130 feet. Until an infrared telescope such as Webb, or NASA's planned NEO Surveyor, measures an asteroid's heat, any size in a flyby alert is only as good as the albedo behind it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will asteroid 2026 WU1 come back?

A JPL query lists no other pass within 0.2 astronomical units (about 78 lunar distances, or 18.6 million miles) between 2026 and 2126, and JPL's Sentry impact-monitoring system returned no entry for the asteroid. With a condition code of 7, those predictions will be recalculated as observatories add measurements.

Can you see an asteroid flyby without a telescope?

Not an asteroid like this one. An absolute magnitude of 24.7 is extremely faint, and at 4.82 million kilometers (3.0 million miles) the asteroid stayed far beyond naked-eye or binocular reach. Because it has already passed, the best remaining use of images of it is archival, since more positions from observatories that imaged it can refine its orbit. Observers planning to image any asteroid can compute its position with JPL's Horizons ephemeris service.

How can you tell whether an asteroid size in a headline was measured?

Check the wording and the data. JPL's close-approach table reports a diameter only when one is known; its documentation says the field is null when unknown, as it was for 2026 WU1, so a number in a headline usually comes from brightness and an assumed albedo, unless a separate measurement such as Webb's infrared observations of 2024 YR4 exists. Treat "doomsday asteroid" framing with the same caution: a 2026 paper in Meteoritics & Planetary Science reviews decades of asteroid misinformation that followed events such as Chelyabinsk.
